To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) momentum strategies earn abnormal profits in the US and other developed countries, but not in developing countries; 2) the abnormal profits are due to the time-varying nature of stock returns, which are predictable based on a set of macroeconomic factors; and 3) the time-varyng nature of stock returns is due to changes in the expected returns of stocks, which are predictable using the same set of macroeconomic variables.

(1) momentum strategies earn abnormal profits in the US stock market; (2) these profits can be explained by the predictability of returns based on macroeconomic variables; (3) the payoffs to momentum are not due to investor overreaction, but

1) the predictability of momentum payoffs is driven by a set of macroeconomic variables; 2) the predictability based on the macroeconomic variables is due to their correlation with time- varying expected returns; and 3) once stock returns are corrected for their time-varying predictability, there is no evidence of momentum profits.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find that momentum profits are largely explained by time-varying risk premia.
we show that momentum profits are not due to investor irrationalities, and that they do not constitute evidence against market efficiency.

we have shown that momentum is related to the macroeconomic cycle, that is, momentum strategies tend to work best when the business cycle is in an expansion phase and momentum strategies tend to underperform when the business cycle enters a contraction phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
momentum is not the result of investor irrationality.
the momentum strategy is a simple, but powerful way of exploiting the time-varying nature of expected returns.
time-varying macroeconomic variables are important determinants of asset returns, and can be used to improve asset pricing models.
